shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, current US$ at market exchange rates (NGDPDPC); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Twelve dollars. {p} That's how far Poland got ahead of Slovakia last year, in the IMF's numbers: income per person, in plain dollars, at market exchange rates. Twenty-eight thousand five hundred and ten for the average Pole, twenty-eight thousand four hundred and ninety-eight for the average Slovak. {pp} For twenty-two years, from 2003 to 2024, Slovakia was ahead. In 2009, it was forty-three percent ahead. {p} This year, the IMF has Poland about three hundred dollars in front. By 2031, about two and a half thousand.

labels.at: Twenty-eight thousand five hundred and ten

shots.narration: In this series, Poland has been passing countries on income adjusted for prices: Portugal, then Japan. This one is different. This is plain money: what the average person's output is worth in dollars on the world market. {p} And on that measure, Poland just passed a neighbor that uses the euro, and that builds more cars per person than any other country on Earth. {pp} <soft>So how did Slovakia get so far ahead, why did Poland need twenty-two years to catch up, and what about Hungary? Poland has passed Hungary three times.</soft>
Quick one before the chart: this is a series, and the next episode is another country Poland just passed. Subscribe so you don't miss it. {p} Now, the long view.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, current US$ at market exchange rates (NGDPDPC); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: In 1995, the three were close: about three thousand six hundred dollars per person in Poland, three thousand eight hundred in Slovakia, four and a half thousand in Hungary. {p} Then Slovakia took off. In 2003 it passed Poland, and kept pulling away. By 2008, the average Slovak produced about eighteen thousand dollars a year, the average Pole about fourteen. {pp} Then 2009. Slovakia joined the euro, and the gap jumped to forty-three percent. Slovakia stayed ahead every single year after that, until 2025.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · real GDP growth, Slovakia (annual %); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Here's Slovakia's economy, year by year, after inflation. {p} From 2004 to 2007, it grew faster every year: about five percent, then six and a half, almost nine, and almost eleven in 2007. That boom was built on factories, above all car factories. Today Slovakia builds about a million cars a year, in a country of about five point four million people. {pp} But look at the right side. Since 2022, Slovakia has grown about two percent at best. Last year and this year, under one percent. Poland: three point seven, then three point four.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · real GDP growth (NGDP_RPCH, compounded)
shots.title: The real race
shots.narration: Over thirty years, the race was closer than the dollars suggest. Since 1995, after inflation, Poland's economy has grown about three times over, Slovakia's about two point six times, and Hungary's has doubled. {p} Slovakia grew faster before 2008. Poland, much faster after: since 2008, about seventy-six percent, against thirty-nine for Slovakia. {pp} So why did Poland need twenty-two years to catch up in dollars? One word: currency.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, PPP, current international $ (PPPPC); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Slovakia uses the euro. Poland kept its own currency, the złoty. And in 2009, the two went opposite ways. {p} Slovakia's economy shrank five and a half percent. Poland's grew two point six: the only economy in the region that didn't shrink. But in dollars, the average Pole's output fell eighteen percent that year, because the złoty fell. The average Slovak's fell eight. {pp} That's the catch with plain dollars: they move with exchange rates. On this chart, adjusted for what money actually buys at home, Poland passed Slovakia back in 2018. This year, by that measure, the average Pole is about twenty-one percent ahead.
And if you're enjoying the series, the subscribe button is right there. {p} Now, Hungary.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, current US$ at market exchange rates (NGDPDPC); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: In 1990, the average Hungarian produced twice as much as the average Pole, in dollars. {p} Poland first passed Hungary in 2012. Hungary took the lead back in 2013. Poland passed again in 2022. Hungary took it back again in 2023, by seventy-nine dollars. {pp} And in 2024, Poland passed a third time. This one looks like it sticks: about three thousand three hundred dollars ahead this year, and almost six thousand by 2031, in the IMF's forecast. {p} Hungary's recent years explain a lot: inflation of seventeen percent in 2023, the highest of the three, and an economy that shrank that year and barely grew in the next two.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, current US$ at market exchange rates (NGDPDPC); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.title: The pass, in plain dollars
shots.narration: So here's the pass, in the IMF's numbers. {p} 2024: Slovakia twenty-five thousand nine hundred and seventy-two dollars per person, Poland twenty-five thousand one hundred and sixty-eight. Slovakia ahead by about eight hundred. {p} 2025: Poland ahead by twelve dollars. This year, by about three hundred. And by 2031, about two and a half thousand, in the IMF's forecast. {pp} One caveat: twelve dollars is nothing. One revision, or one bad year for the złoty, could flip it back. But the gap has shrunk from forty-three percent in 2009 to nothing.

stats.at: twenty-five thousand nine hundred and seventy-two
stats.label: Slovakia, 2024

stats.at: twenty-five thousand one hundred and sixty-eight
stats.label: Poland, 2024

stats.at: about two and a half thousand
stats.label: Poland ahead, 2031 (IMF)

shots.narration: Zoom out to the four Visegrád countries: Poland, Czechia, Slovakia and Hungary. {p} In 1995, Poland was the poorest of the four in plain dollars. In 2025, it moved to second. {p} Only Czechia is still ahead: about thirty-nine and a half thousand dollars per person this year, against thirty-one in Poland. That's seventy-nine percent, and the IMF has Poland at eighty-six percent of Czechia by 2031.

<soft>So, your guess: does Poland stay ahead of Slovakia this time, or does the złoty flip it back, the way Hungary flipped it in 2023?</soft> Tell me in the comments. {p} If you're watching from Slovakia: does this match what you see? {p} If you're in Poland: did you know Slovakia was ever this far ahead? {p} I read every comment.
And if you missed it, this is where the series took off: the year Poland passed Japan, adjusted for prices. It's right here. {p} I'm Chartbound. See you in the next one.

yt.title: Poland Just Passed Slovakia. By $12.
yt.description:
Income per person in plain US dollars (IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026): Slovakia was ahead of Poland every year from 2003 to 2024 — 43% ahead in 2009. In 2025: Poland $28,510, Slovakia $28,498. A $12 lead, ~$300 this year and ~$2,500 by 2031 in the IMF's forecast. Slovakia's car-led sprint (10.8% growth in 2007), why the złoty kept Poland behind in dollars (adjusted for prices, Poland passed Slovakia back in 2018), Hungary passed three times (2012, 2022, 2024), and where Poland now stands among the Visegrád four.

Sources: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 (NGDPDPC, PPPPC, NGDP_RPCH, LP, LUR, GGXWDG_NGDP, PCPIPCH). 2026+ figures are IMF estimates and forecasts.
